Pathology-2.question: ১) Which organisms contain ribosomes, do not have a rigid cell wall but cannot be grown on inanimate culture?
Pathology-2.exp:
Chlamydia are obligate intracellular bacteria. They:

  • Contain both DNA and RNA

  • Possess 70S ribosomes

  • Lack a rigid peptidoglycan cell wall (although they have an outer membrane)

  • Cannot be grown on artificial (inanimate) culture media and require living cells (e.g., cell culture, embryonated eggs).

Rapid Recall

  • Chlamydia → Obligate intracellular

  • Mycoplasma → No cell wall but grows on PPLO medium

  • Rickettsia → Obligate intracellular + Gram-negative cell wall

  • Viruses → No ribosomes

Pathology-2.question: ২) A patient came to you with H/O. a firm 12mm ulcerated lesion with smooth edges to the penis. The patient denies any pain. what will be the cause?
Pathology-2.exp:
The patient has a firm, painless, ulcerated penile lesion with smooth edges, which is the classic hard chancre of primary syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum.

Rapid Recall

  • Painless hard chancre → Treponema pallidum

  • Painful vesicles → HSV-2

  • Painful soft chancre → Haemophilus ducreyi

  • Painless ulcer + painful buboes → LGV (Chlamydia trachomatis L1–L3)

Pathology-2.question: ৩) You are asked to review a 65-year-old lady’s legs preoperatively. You diagnose cellulitis. What is the most common causative organism?
Pathology-2.exp:
Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue. The most common causative organism is Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). It typically presents with diffuse erythema, warmth, swelling, tenderness, and poorly demarcated margins.

Staphylococcus aureus is also a common cause, particularly in cases associated with purulent cellulitis, abscesses, or skin trauma, but S. pyogenes remains the single most common cause of non-purulent cellulitis.

High-Yield

  • Cellulitis → Streptococcus pyogenes

  • Purulent cellulitis/abscess → Staphylococcus aureus

  • Erysipelas → Streptococcus pyogenes

  • Gas gangrene → Clostridium perfringens

Rapid Recall

  • Cellulitis → Group A Streptococcus

  • Abscess → Staphylococcus aureus

  • Erysipelas → Streptococcus pyogenes

  • Gas in tissues → Clostridium perfringens

Pathology-2.question: ৪) Rose gardeners commonly affected by-
Pathology-2.exp:
Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus that causes sporotrichosis, also known as "rose gardener's disease." Infection occurs when the fungus is inoculated into the skin through rose thorns, splinters, or other plant material. It typically presents as a nodular lesion that spreads along the lymphatic channels (lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis).

High-Yield

  • Rose gardener → Sporothrix schenckii

  • Dimorphic fungus

  • Route: Traumatic implantation from rose thorns

  • Characteristic: Nodules spreading along lymphatics

Rapid Recall

  • Rose thorn → Sporothrix schenckii

  • Cat exposure → Sporotrichosis (can also transmit)

  • "Sporothrix = Spine (thorn) + Lymphatics"

  • Treatment: Itraconazole (first-line for cutaneous disease)

Pathology-2.question: ৫) Curdy white discharge found in-
Pathology-2.exp:
Candida vulvovaginitis classically presents with thick, white, curdy ("cottage cheese") vaginal discharge, along with intense vulval itching, soreness, and erythema. The vaginal pH is usually normal (≤4.5).

Rapid Recall

  • Curdy white → Candida

  • Frothy green → Trichomonas

  • Fishy gray → Gardnerella

  • Mucopurulent cervicitis → Chlamydia

Pathology-2.question: ৬) Predisposing factor for toxic shock syndrome
৭) Endocarditis on prosthetic heart valve is caused by
Pathology-2.exp: Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis, especially early prosthetic valve endocarditis. It forms biofilms on prosthetic materials, allowing it to adhere to artificial valves and resist host defenses and antibiotics.

Pathology-2.question: ৮) Cells not involved in innate immunity
Pathology-2.exp:
T lymphocytes are the principal cells of the adaptive (acquired) immune system, recognizing specific antigens through T-cell receptors. They are not part of innate immunity.

In contrast, neutrophils, natural killer (NK) cells, and macrophages are key components of the innate immune system.

Rapid Recall

  • Innate → Neutrophils, NK cells, Macrophages

  • Adaptive → T cells, B cells

  • NK cells kill without prior sensitization

  • T lymphocytes require antigen-specific activation

Pathology-2.question: ৯) Factor that limits entry of microorganism into body
Pathology-2.exp:
Defensins are small cationic antimicrobial peptides produced by epithelial cells and neutrophils. They are present on the skin and mucosal surfaces, where they kill microorganisms and prevent their entry into the body, making them an important first-line innate immune defense.

High-Yield

  • First-line barrier molecules: Defensins, lysozyme, secretory IgA

  • Complement: Opsonization (C3b), chemotaxis (C5a), lysis (MAC, C5b-9)

  • Transferrin/Lactoferrin: Restrict bacterial growth by sequestering iron

Rapid Recall

  • Entry barrier → Defensins

  • Iron binding → Transferrin

  • Opsonization → C3b

  • Fever → IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α mediated systemic response

Pathology-2.question: ১০) Professional antigen presenting cell
Pathology-2.exp:
The professional antigen-presenting cells (APCs) are:

  • Dendritic cells (most potent)

  • Macrophages

  • B lymphocytes

Among the given options, B lymphocyte is the only professional APC. It presents antigen to CD4⁺ T helper cells via MHC class II molecules.

High-Yield

Professional APCs:

  • Dendritic cell (most effective)

  • Macrophage

  • B lymphocyte

Mnemonic: "DMB" = Dendritic, Macrophage, B cell

Rapid Recall

  • Best APC → Dendritic cell

  • Professional APCs → Dendritic cells, Macrophages, B cells

  • MHC II → APCs → CD4⁺ T helper cells

  • MHC I → All nucleated cells → CD8⁺ T cells

Pathology-2.question: ১১) Which Ig can cross placenta?
Pathology-2.exp:
IgG is the only immunoglobulin class that crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the fetus. Transfer occurs via the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) on placental syncytiotrophoblasts, predominantly during the third trimester.

High-Yield

  • Placenta → IgG

  • Breast milk (colostrum) → Secretory IgA

  • First antibody produced → IgM

  • Allergy & parasitic infection → IgE

Rapid Recall

  • G Goes through the placenta → IgG

  • A = Aliment (breast milk) → IgA

  • M = Makes first response → IgM

  • E = Eosinophils & allergy → IgE

Pathology-2.question: ১২) UTI in young women is mostly caused by
১৩) Immune mediated disease caused by S. pyogenes
১৪) Which streptococcus causes neonatal sepsis & meningitis?
Pathology-2.exp:
Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) is the leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis. It is acquired vertically from the maternal genital tract during labor and delivery.

High-Yield

  • Group B Streptococcus (GBS) = S. agalactiae

  • Neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis

  • Maternal screening at 35–37 weeks

  • Intrapartum IV penicillin prevents early-onset neonatal GBS disease

Rapid Recall

  • GBS → Neonatal sepsis & meningitis

  • GAS (S. pyogenes) → Pharyngitis, rheumatic fever

  • S. bovis → Colon cancer association

  • Viridans → Dental caries, subacute endocarditis

Pathology-2.question: ১৫) Example of type-III hypersensitivity reaction is-
Pathology-2.exp:
Type III hypersensitivity is an immune complex-mediated reaction. Circulating antigen–antibody (IgG/IgM) complexes deposit in tissues, activate complement, and cause inflammation.

Serum sickness is the classic example of a Type III hypersensitivity reaction.

Rapid Recall

  • Type I → IgE

  • Type II → Antibody-mediated

  • Type III → Immune complexes → Serum sickness

  • Type IV → T-cell mediated → Delayed hypersensitivity

Pathology-2.question: ১৬) Most common location of secondary tuberculosis of lung is-
Pathology-2.exp:
Secondary (post-primary/reactivation) pulmonary tuberculosis most commonly affects the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes (apex) because these regions have the highest oxygen tension, which favors the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Rapid Recall

  • Primary TB → Ghon focus + hilar nodes

  • Secondary TB → Apex (upper lobe), cavitation

  • Reason → High oxygen tension favors mycobacterial growth

Pathology-2.question: ১৭) Which is obligate intracellular organism?
Pathology-2.exp:
Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium because it cannot produce sufficient ATP and depends on the host cell for energy. It has a unique life cycle with:

  • Elementary body (EB): Infectious form

  • Reticulate body (RB): Replicative form

High-Yield

Obligate intracellular bacteria:

  • Chlamydia spp.

  • Rickettsia spp.

  • Coxiella burnetii (intracellular but can be cultured in specialized systems)

Rapid Recall

  • Chlamydia → Obligate intracellular

  • Rickettsia → Obligate intracellular

  • Mycoplasma → No cell wall

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae → Intracellular in neutrophils, but not obligate intracellular

Pathology-2.question: ১৮) Which streptococcus is lancet shaped?
১৯) Which organism causes endocarditis following dental procedure?
২০) Skin can be penetrated by
Pathology-2.exp:
Strongyloides stercoralis infects humans when the filariform (L3) larvae penetrate intact skin, usually through contact with contaminated soil. The larvae then migrate via the bloodstream to the lungs and eventually reach the intestine.

High-Yield

Helminths that penetrate skin:

  • Strongyloides stercoralis

  • Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus)

  • Schistosoma cercariae

Rapid Recall

  • Skin penetration → Strongyloides, Hookworm, Schistosoma

  • Ascaris → Ingestion of eggs

  • Trichuris → Ingestion of eggs

  • Echinococcus → Ingestion of dog tapeworm eggs

Pathology-2.question: ২১) The most common cause of “traveler’s diarrhea” is
Pathology-2.exp:
The most common cause of traveler's diarrhea is Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC). It produces heat-labile (LT) and/or heat-stable (ST) enterotoxins, causing watery diarrhea without invasion of the intestinal mucosa.

High-Yield

  • Traveler's diarrhea → ETEC

  • Toxins: LT (↑cAMP) and ST (↑cGMP)

  • Clinical feature: Watery, non-bloody diarrhea

  • No mucosal invasion

Rapid Recall

  • Traveler's diarrhea → ETEC

  • Cholera → Profuse rice-water stool

  • Shigella → Bloody diarrhea

  • Rotavirus → Infantile gastroenteritis

Pathology-2.question: ২২) Listeria monocytogenes most frequently causes which of the following infections?
Pathology-2.exp:
Listeria monocytogenes most commonly causes meningitis and meningoencephalitis, particularly in:

  • Neonates

  • Pregnant women

  • Elderly

  • Immunocompromised patients

It is a Gram-positive, facultative intracellular bacillus with tumbling motility and is transmitted through contaminated food (unpasteurized dairy products, soft cheeses, deli meats).

High-Yield

  • Organism: Listeria monocytogenes

  • Disease: Meningitis, neonatal sepsis

  • Risk groups: Neonates, pregnant women, elderly, immunocompromised

  • Treatment: Ampicillin ± gentamicin (Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins)

Rapid Recall

  • Listeria → Meningitis

  • Neonate + Pregnant + Elderly + Immunocompromised

  • Tumbling motility

  • Ampicillin is the drug of choice

Pathology-2.question: ২৩) Smallest free living organism
২৪) Which one remains positive for life in syphilis?
২৫) RNA nucleocapsid virus
২৬) ESR is increased disproportionately to CRP in -
Pathology-2.exp:
In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the ESR is often markedly elevated, whereas the CRP is usually normal or only mildly increased, unless there is concurrent infection, significant serositis, or synovitis. This discordance is a classic clinical clue.

High-Yield

  • High ESR + normal/mildly raised CRP → Think SLE

  • High ESR + high CRP → Think bacterial infection or active inflammatory arthritis

  • Markedly raised CRP in an SLE patient should raise suspicion of infection

Rapid Recall

  • SLE → ESR ↑↑, CRP ↔/slightly ↑

  • Bacterial infection → ESR ↑, CRP ↑↑

  • Multiple myeloma → ESR ↑↑ (rouleaux formation)

Pathology-2.question: ২৭) Immune complex mediated hypersensitivity
Pathology-2.exp:
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a Type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. Antigen-antibody (immune) complexes are deposited in tissues, activating complement and causing inflammation and tissue damage.

Rapid Recall

  • Type I → Allergy (IgE)

  • Type II → Goodpasture

  • Type III → SLE

  • Type IV → Type 1 diabetes, Contact dermatitis

Pathology-2.question: ২৮) Which is the most common form of graft rejection?
Pathology-2.exp:
Acute cellular rejection is the most common form of graft rejection. It is T-cell mediated (Type IV hypersensitivity) and usually occurs days to weeks after transplantation, although it may occur later if immunosuppression is inadequate.

Rapid Recall

  • Most common graft rejection → Acute cellular rejection

  • Hyperacute → Preformed antibodies

  • Acute cellular → T cells

  • Chronic → Fibrosis + graft vasculopathy

Pathology-2.question: ২৯) Kaposi’s sarcoma is recurrent infection of
৩০) Initial site of infection of VZV in
৩১) Antigenic shift & drift occurs in
৩২) Transplacental transmission occurs in
Pathology-2.exp:
Treponema pallidum readily crosses the placenta, usually after the first trimester (≈16 weeks of gestation), causing congenital syphilis. This is the classic example of transplacental transmission.

High-Yield

Common transplacental (congenital) infections – TORCH:

  • Toxoplasmosis

  • Others (including Syphilis, Varicella, Parvovirus B19)

  • Rubella

  • CMV

  • HSV (mostly intrapartum)

Rapid Recall

  • Syphilis → Transplacental

  • HBV → Perinatal (during delivery)

  • HIV → In utero + Intrapartum + Breastfeeding

  • Chlamydia → Birth canal transmission

Pathology-2.question: ৩৩) Which disease produces vesicular rash?
Pathology-2.exp:
Chickenpox (Varicella-zoster virus, VZV) characteristically causes a generalized vesicular rash described as "dew drops on a rose petal." Lesions appear in different stages simultaneously (macules, papules, vesicles, pustules, and crusts).

Rapid Recall

  • Chickenpox → Vesicular rash

  • Measles → Koplik spots

  • Rubella → Postauricular lymphadenopathy

  • Parvovirus B19 → Slapped-cheek rash

Pathology-2.question: ৩৪) Which marker is positive in immunized people without infection?
Pathology-2.exp:
Anti-HBs (hepatitis B surface antibody) is the marker of immunity to hepatitis B. In individuals who have been vaccinated without natural infection, only Anti-HBs is positive. They do not develop antibodies to the core antigen because the vaccine contains only HBsAg, not HBcAg.

Rapid Recall

  • Vaccinated only → Anti-HBs (+)

  • Acute infection → HBsAg +, Anti-HBc IgM +

  • Past natural infection → Anti-HBs +, Anti-HBc IgG +

  • HBsAg = Infection; Anti-HBs = Immunity

Pathology-2.question: ৩৫) Rash is not a prominent feature in
৩৬) Antigen testing of blood and cerebrospinal fluid is most useful in the diagnosis of
Pathology-2.exp:
Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) detection in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is the most sensitive and specific rapid test for diagnosing cryptococcosis, especially cryptococcal meningitis in patients with HIV/AIDS or other immunocompromised states.

High-Yield

  • Cryptococcus neoformans

    • Encapsulated yeast

    • Causes meningitis in immunocompromised patients

    • India ink: Encapsulated budding yeast in CSF

    • CrAg (serum/CSF): Most sensitive diagnostic test

    • Treatment: Amphotericin B + Flucytosine → Fluconazole

Rapid Recall

  • CSF antigen test → Cryptococcosis

  • India ink positive → Cryptococcus

  • Encapsulated yeast → Cryptococcus neoformans

  • AIDS + Meningitis → Think Cryptococcus

Pathology-2.question: ৩৭) Activation of complement in any pathways results in activation of
Pathology-2.exp:
All three complement pathways—classical, lectin, and alternative—converge at the activation of C3. Formation of C3 convertase is the central event in complement activation, leading to cleavage of C3 into C3a and C3b.

  • C3a → Anaphylatoxin (promotes inflammation)

  • C3b → Opsonization and formation of C5 convertase

Rapid Recall

  • Common convergence point → C3

  • C3b → Opsonization

  • C3a, C5a → Anaphylatoxins

  • C5b–C9 → Membrane Attack Complex (MAC)

Pathology-2.question: ৩৮) Which is key determinant of antigen presentation to T-cell?
Pathology-2.exp:
The Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) complex, also known as the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC), is the key determinant of antigen presentation to T cells.

  • HLA Class I (A, B, C) presents endogenous antigens to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells.

  • HLA Class II (DP, DQ, DR) presents exogenous antigens to CD4⁺ helper T cells.

Rapid Recall

  • HLA = Antigen presentation

  • Class I → CD8

  • Class II → CD4

  • CTLA-4 → T-cell inhibition

  • PTPN22 → Autoimmunity gene

Pathology-2.question: ৩৯) Diagnosis of hereditary angioedema can be confirmed by measurement of level of
Pathology-2.exp:
Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is caused by deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor (C1-INH). The confirmatory test is measurement of the C1 inhibitor level and/or functional activity.

Although C4 is persistently low and is an excellent screening test, the diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating reduced or dysfunctional C1 inhibitor.

High-Yield

Test Result in Hereditary Angioedema
C1 inhibitor level/function ↓ (Confirmatory)
C4 ↓ (Screening test)
C3 Normal
IgE Normal

Rapid Recall

  • HAE → C1 inhibitor deficiency/dysfunction

  • Screening → Low C4

  • Confirmation → Low or dysfunctional C1 inhibitor

  • Bradykinin-mediated → No urticaria, poor response to antihistamines or adrenaline

Pathology-2.question: ৪০) Organism produces flaccid paralysis-
Pathology-2.exp:
Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum neurotoxin, which blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, resulting in descending flaccid paralysis.

Rapid Recall

  • Botulinum → Flaccid paralysis

  • Tetanus → Spastic paralysis

  • Botulinum toxin → ↓ Acetylcholine release

  • Tetanospasmin → ↓ GABA & Glycine release

Pathology-2.question: ৪১) A patient came to you with H/O contamination by HIV positive woman. Western Blot test is done. It is indeterminate. What will you do now?
Pathology-2.exp:
An indeterminate Western blot result is neither positive nor negative. It may occur during the window period of early HIV infection, when antibodies have not yet fully developed. In such cases, the appropriate approach is to repeat the HIV antibody test (or Western blot) after about 1 month (and continue follow-up testing as indicated by current guidelines).

High-Yield

  • Positive ELISA → Confirmatory test (historically Western blot)

  • Indeterminate Western blot → Repeat testing after 2–4 weeks (≈1 month)

  • Current practice: Fourth-generation HIV Ag/Ab assays followed by an HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation assay; if results remain discordant, HIV nucleic acid testing (NAT) is recommended.

Rapid Recall

  • Indeterminate Western blot → Repeat after 1 month

  • ELISA → Screening

  • Western blot → Historical confirmatory test

  • Modern algorithm → 4th-generation HIV test + differentiation assay ± NAT

Pathology-2.question: ৪২) Ground itch is associated with-
Pathology-2.exp:
Ground itch is an itchy papulovesicular dermatitis that occurs when the filariform (L3) larvae of hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus) penetrate the skin, usually of the bare feet after contact with contaminated soil.

High-Yield

  • Ground itch → Hookworm (L3 filariform larva)

  • Skin penetration → Filariform larva

  • Adults → Small intestine → Iron deficiency anemia

  • Infective stage → Filariform larva (L3)

Rapid Recall

  • Ground itch → Hookworm

  • Hookworm infective stage → Filariform larva

  • Ascaris infective stage → Embryonated egg

  • Strongyloides also enters through skin

Pathology-2.question: ৪৩) Most common neoplasm associated with HIV-
Pathology-2.exp:
Kaposi sarcoma is the classic and most common neoplasm associated with HIV/AIDS in traditional MBBS/FCPS microbiology and pathology examinations. It is caused by Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) and typically presents as violaceous (purple) skin or mucosal lesions.

Rapid Recall

  • HIV + Purple skin lesions → Kaposi sarcoma

  • Kaposi sarcoma → HHV-8

  • Burkitt lymphoma → EBV, c-MYC translocation

  • Primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS → EBV

Pathology-2.question: ৪৪) Sterility due to bilateral orchitis may occur in
৪৫) Negri bodies are found in
৪৬) The principal sites of tissue reaction in Ascariasis
Pathology-2.exp:
During ascariasis, the most significant tissue reaction occurs in the lungs when Ascaris lumbricoides larvae migrate through the pulmonary capillaries and alveoli. This migration causes eosinophilic pneumonitis (Löffler syndrome), characterized by fever, cough, wheeze, transient pulmonary infiltrates, and eosinophilia.

High-Yield

  • Ascaris infective stage: Embryonated egg

  • Larval migration: Intestine → Liver → Lung → Trachea → Intestine

  • Pulmonary phase: Löffler syndrome

  • Adult worms: Small intestine

Rapid Recall

  • Ascaris → Lung → Löffler syndrome

  • Hookworm → Ground itch

  • Strongyloides → Skin penetration + Autoinfection

  • Adult Ascaris → Small intestine

Pathology-2.question: ৪৭) The vector and definitive host for plasmodia is the
Pathology-2.exp:
The female Anopheles mosquito is both the vector and the definitive host of Plasmodium because sexual reproduction (sporogony) occurs in the mosquito. Humans are the intermediate host, where asexual reproduction (schizogony) takes place.

Rapid Recall

  • Female Anopheles → Vector + Definitive host

  • Human → Intermediate host

  • Infective stage to humans → Sporozoite

  • Infective stage to mosquito → Gametocyte

Pathology-2.question: ৪৮) Which plasmodium species causes malignant malaria?
Pathology-2.exp:
Plasmodium falciparum causes malignant tertian malaria, the most severe form of malaria. It can infect red blood cells of all ages, leading to high parasitemia and serious complications such as cerebral malaria, severe anemia, acute kidney injury, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, and pulmonary edema.

Rapid Recall

  • Falciparum → Malignant malaria

  • Vivax & Ovale → Benign tertian + hypnozoites

  • Malariae → Quartan fever (72 hours)

Pathology-2.question: ৪৯) Site of damage in blackwater fever
Pathology-2.exp:
Blackwater fever is a severe complication of Plasmodium falciparum malaria characterized by massive intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria (giving urine a black color), and acute kidney injury (AKI). The kidney is the principal organ damaged due to hemoglobin-induced tubular injury and reduced renal perfusion.

High-Yield

  • Cause: Severe P. falciparum malaria

  • Features: Hemoglobinuria ("black urine"), severe hemolysis, anemia, acute kidney injury

  • Complication: Renal failure

Rapid Recall

  • Blackwater fever → P. falciparum

  • Black urine → Hemoglobinuria

  • Main organ damaged → Kidney

  • Cerebral malaria → Brain (different severe complication)

Pathology-2.question: ৫০) Characteristic of kala-azar
Pathology-2.exp:
Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is caused by Leishmania donovani. The most characteristic clinical feature is massive splenomegaly, often accompanied by prolonged irregular fever, weight loss, hepatomegaly, pancytopenia, and skin darkening ("kala-azar").

High-Yield

  • Organism: Leishmania donovani

  • Vector: Female sandfly (Phlebotomus)

  • Diagnostic stage: Amastigotes (LD bodies) in splenic, bone marrow, or lymph node aspirate

  • Hallmark: Massive splenomegaly with pancytopenia

Rapid Recall

  • Kala-azar → Leishmania donovani

  • Vector → Sandfly

  • Diagnostic finding → LD bodies (amastigotes)

  • Most characteristic feature → Massive splenomegaly
